speaker: Tano Santos
text: Thank you so much.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I know you guys are incredibly excited to be here, and I know it’s not because of me, but rather because of our guest today, who I will introduce shortly.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Before we start with the interview, let me take a couple of minutes to tell you that, as always at this time of year, the Heilbrunn year is up and running in full swing.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: The students, some of whom are here, have already taken my Modern Value class.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: They’re taking the Applied Value Investing class, their Credit Superhighway, all the electives.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: We’re having a blast.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: They’re all absolutely wonderful.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: In addition, we have a new initiative this year in the Heilbrunn Center.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: We launched our first Global Value Investor program, and the first cohort of that program, a joint effort with Columbia Business School Executive Education, is here.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: These are all the wonderful friends from China who are visiting us this year.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Thank you so much for being here.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Michael and I — I get asked this question a little too often — are already working on a new season of the Value Investing with Legends podcast.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Episodes will be coming soon, so that is something to look forward to.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: We made our new stock selections for the student portfolio, the Tom Russo student portfolio.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: What did we buy this year?

text: Equifax, Humana.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: What else?

text: We bought the great Japanese bicycle company, Shimano, a classic value play if there was one; Copart, an online auction company; Perimeter Solutions, fire solutions.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: A lot of fun things.

text: As always, you can download all the reports the students have done over the years on the different companies.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: It’s a wonderful resource, and I very much encourage you to look at that.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I want to single out a wonderful member of our community.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I’m always amazed by Tom Russo’s generosity with the Heilbrunn Center, not only because of the student portfolio, but because of everything he does for the program, and in particular this year, making sure that our friend Li Lu could be here, for which we’re always thankful.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: We just had a wonderful week, as I told you a moment ago.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: With this new program, the Global Value Investor program, Andrew Gundlach and Kristin Gilbertson put on a show for them, which I also want to acknowledge publicly.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Finally, we’re getting ready for a terrific CIMA conference.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: It’s amazing, the names that are coming this year.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: We’re going to have Howard Marks, Bill Ackman will be there, Josh Wolfe of Lux Capital will be there, Samantha McLemore from Patient Capital.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I very much hope to see many of you there.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Now, to the main event.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Li Lu, of course, needs no introduction, as he’s truly one of the great modern value investing legends.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: He’s the founder and chairman of Himalaya Capital, which he founded in 1997.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: He has built an enormous record of performance in the last 30 years.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Li Lu, as many of you know, is one of our most distinguished alums.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: He graduated with a law degree, an MBA degree, and a BA from Columbia College, because why get just one degree when you can get three?

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Apparently, this was how he thought about it.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: His personal story is well known.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I won’t repeat it here.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Li Lu is famous as an early investor in BYD and many of the great Chinese names, and we’ll have the opportunity to discuss issues related to the Chinese stock market today.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: First of all, Li Lu, welcome, and thank you so much for being here.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Thank you, Tano.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I’m going to talk for about 15 minutes, and then I’ll open it up for questions.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I’m going to ask you to keep them short and to the point, and I will be ruthless.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: If you take more time than I consider necessary to get your point across, I’ll cut you off and give you a nasty look.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Keep them short, because I’m sure there will be many questions.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Li Lu, I want to start here.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: As I said, you are one of the great names in modern value investing.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: You’re deeply intertwined with the story of value investing at Columbia Business School.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: We were talking about that over lunch.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: You were there at the very beginning when Bruce was launching this program.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: We know of your friendship and partnership with Charlie and Warren, and how many things you guys did together.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: We will be celebrating 30 years of the founding of Himalaya Capital next year, which is a remarkable achievement.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I want to start here.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I want you to tell us a little bit: What have you learned about value investing, and where do you think we are today?

speaker: Tano Santos
text: What is the thing you wish you had known at the beginning?

speaker: Tano Santos
text: What is the lesson we have now that we didn’t have when you were studying these ideas at Columbia Business School?

speaker: Li Lu
text: Thank you, Tano.

speaker: Li Lu
text: First of all, thank you all for being here.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It is such a wonderful occasion.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Back when I was a student, as well as a young professional, I also attended a few of those luncheons.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It was the highlight.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I hope I do some justice now, 30 years later.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The discipline of value investing started with Columbia.

speaker: Li Lu
text: When Ben Graham first started his classes, it was almost 90 years ago.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Of course, he practiced 10 or 20 years before that, so we call it a 100-year-old discipline.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It really has evolved, but some of the core principles have not and have become timeless.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If I have to distill the main principles for the discipline of value investing, I would say there are six in my mind.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Three come directly from Ben Graham, the namesake of today’s lunch; one each from Warren and Charlie; and we add a small twist — you could call that the sixth.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Here are the six basic principles in my mind that have guided our discipline, at least our practice, over the last 33 years.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Ben Graham laid it out pretty quickly as he started this discipline with three basic ideas.

speaker: Li Lu
text: A stock is a piece of ownership, not a piece of paper to trade around.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Buying stock is really the same as buying a company.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Secondly, the market is there to serve you, not to instruct you, which is a profound insight if you are in the midst of market activities.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Thirdly, investing is about predicting the future, which is inherently unpredictable.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Therefore, you always want to require a margin of safety that will help protect the downside as well as make a better upside.

speaker: Li Lu
text: When Warren practiced, I think he added this further discipline, which I call a circle of competence.

speaker: Li Lu
text: All of us are probably predisposed to have certain interests, and over time you develop particular expertise and try to study more and make it better.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The most important concept of a circle of competence is knowing the edge of it, because most of us are wired to think we know a little more than we actually do.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Understanding the edge is as important as understanding what is inside it.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Charlie had this idea that you’ve got to fish where the fish are.

speaker: Li Lu
text: He was a lifelong fisherman, and that is a wonderful analogy for the actual market.

speaker: Li Lu
text: There are certain markets, industries, and businesses that draw a lot of attention.

speaker: Li Lu
text: With that competition, your returns are averaged out.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Then there are other industries, businesses, countries, or markets that don’t attract enough attention and have far fewer fishermen.

speaker: Li Lu
text: You do way better to fish where the fish are.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It’s a simple idea, but in practice it is amazingly effective.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Lastly, over my own 33 years of practice as a global investor, applying the principles of value investing on a global basis at a time when global commerce is becoming one single market.

speaker: Li Lu
text: One insight we have is that wealth, in the end, is really the percentage ownership of global purchasing power.

speaker: Li Lu
text: It isn’t expressed, especially in the modern economy, in the amount of gold, diamonds, or currencies of any kind.

speaker: Li Lu
text: With inflation, all of those will dissipate over time.

speaker: Li Lu
text: What is important is what you can buy with it, what you can use it for.

speaker: Li Lu
text: A better measurement of wealth is your percentage ownership of global purchasing power.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The way we express that is by buying great businesses in the most dynamic economies at advantageous prices, waiting long enough for value to be created over time, and sharing proportionally in the upside.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Here are the six basic ideas that I think can withstand the test of time and will serve everyone well.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I like this last point very much.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I’m already deviating from the script you and I agreed on, because I think going forward, keeping an eye on that purchasing power is going to be key if we’re not able to control inflation in the presence of these fiscal challenges.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: If we have time, we’ll come back to this.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Sure.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: I want to get a question in before we run out of time, for the benefit of my students in the room.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: This is my prerogative as the person asking you the questions, so we’ll get this out of the way.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Value investing as a practice has seen ups and downs.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: It’s been improving conceptually over time, with Bruce, your leadership, and many of the people in this room as well.

speaker: Tano Santos
text: What is the future of the equity analyst in the age of AI?

speaker: Tano Santos
text: Do you think we can still teach what we do at Columbia Business School going forward?

speaker: Li Lu
text: Let me answer that in two parts.

speaker: Li Lu
text: First, what investors do, and then let’s talk about AI separately.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If you look at market participants, there are basically four different kinds of people.

speaker: Li Lu
text: There are investors who stay with the company over time for value creation.

speaker: Li Lu
text: There are also people who arbitrage the rights and wrongs of market pricing.

speaker: Li Lu
text: In Ben Graham’s terms, as a realist, you buy from the pessimist and sell to the optimist.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Those are the arbitrageurs.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Then you have people who are in it mostly for speculation, mostly guessing what other people would buy or sell in a certain security.

speaker: Li Lu
text: They don’t care about either the value pricing of the security or value creation.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Then there are the brokers and market makers who facilitate all that.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Most people are not necessarily purists.

speaker: Li Lu
text: They encompass somewhat of all four.

speaker: Li Lu
text: If you have indexing, it is exactly that average, in a sense.

speaker: Li Lu
text: But value investors are into getting the right pricing discovery and waiting for value creation over a period of time.

speaker: Li Lu
text: I would say Ben Graham was more of an arbitrageur, and Warren is using the arbitrage price, but mostly for value creation.

speaker: Li Lu
text: The social benefit of all different ones is also quite interesting.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Speculators, by definition, don’t stay there long enough for any of the value changes or creations, so they add up to roughly zero.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Whatever is made and lost probably adds up exactly to that.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Net to society, it is a cost to the functioning of the market.

speaker: Li Lu
text: Brokerage and market making are also a cost to the functioning of the market.
